tagline: Land of a thousand lakes and saunas
overview:
Finland stretches from the Baltic Sea almost to the Arctic Ocean in the far north of Europe, squeezed between Sweden, Norway, and Russia. It is a little smaller than Montana but has about 188,000 lakes and roughly 180,000 islands, so from the air the country looks like a green cloth spattered with blue. Forests cover about three-quarters of the land. The capital, Helsinki, sits on a peninsula in the south, a city of harbors, granite, and clean modern design.

About 5.6 million Finns live here, mostly in the south. Finnish is the main language, a tongue related to Estonian and distantly to Hungarian, with long compound words and no articles; Swedish is the second official language, spoken along the coast, and the Sami people of Lapland speak their own languages. Finland is a parliamentary republic and a member of the European Union, and it joined NATO in 2023. Finns have topped world happiness rankings year after year, thanks to trust, excellent free schools, nature at everyone's doorstep, and about three million saunas.
landAndNature: Finland is mostly low and flat, shaped by glaciers that scraped the bedrock and left behind lakes, eskers, and boulders. The largest lake, Saimaa, is a labyrinth of islands and channels where the endangered Saimaa ringed seal lives, one of the rarest seals on Earth. In the north, Lapland rises into rounded fells; Halti, the highest point at 1,324 meters, sits on the Norwegian border. Above the Arctic Circle the sun never sets for weeks in summer and barely rises in midwinter, when the northern lights ripple across the sky. Brown bears, wolves, lynx, wolverines, and about 200,000 reindeer, herded by the Sami, live in the forests and tundra. The Baltic coast freezes in cold winters, and the Åland Islands form an archipelago of thousands of rocky isles.
peopleAndCulture: The sauna is the heart of Finnish life: families sweat together in wood-heated rooms, then plunge into a lake or roll in snow, and even apartment buildings and parliament have saunas. Foods include rye bread, salmon soup, Karelian pies filled with rice, reindeer stew in the north, and squeaky bread cheese with cloudberry jam. Midsummer bonfires blaze on lake shores, and at Christmas Finns claim Santa Claus lives on Korvatunturi fell in Lapland. Ice hockey is the national sport, and Finland has produced champion rally and Formula One drivers and ski jumpers. Composer Jean Sibelius, architect Alvar Aalto, and the Moomin books of Tove Jansson are national treasures. Finns are famously quiet and comfortable with silence, and coffee consumption is among the highest in the world.
history: Hunters reached Finland as the ice retreated about 10,000 years ago. From the 1100s Sweden gradually took control, bringing Christianity and Swedish law, and Finland stayed part of Sweden for about 600 years. In 1809 Russia won it in a war and ruled it as a grand duchy with some self-government, during which Finnish literature and national feeling grew, helped by the epic poem collection the Kalevala. Finland declared independence in 1917 as Russia collapsed into revolution, then suffered a short civil war. In the Winter War of 1939 and 1940 Finns fought off a far larger Soviet invasion but lost territory. After World War II Finland stayed neutral between East and West, built a strong welfare state, and joined the European Union in 1995. Russia's invasion of Ukraine led Finland to join NATO in 2023.
funFacts: Finland has about three million saunas for 5.6 million people, more than it has cars.
Finns hold the Wife Carrying World Championships every year, where the prize is the wife's weight in beer.
Finnish schools give almost no homework and start formal schooling at age seven, yet rank among the best in the world.
The country drinks more coffee per person than any other, about four cups a day on average.
Finland has more heavy metal bands per person than any other country, with more than 50 bands per 100,000 people.
